title: ICE Arrests Two on Sea-Tac Jetway, Delaying Los Angeles-Bound Flight
excerpt: Washington's governor called the jetway arrests 'deeply un-American' and urged airlines to push ICE out of airports; Alaska Airlines said it had no advance notice.
body:
• ICE officers arrested two people on the jetway of Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning, November 21, as passengers boarded for Los Angeles.
  • ICE said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, who it said had overstayed his visa; a second passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was arrested after, ICE said, she threw hot coffee at officers, and may be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
  • The flight, scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., left at 11 a.m.; Alaska Airlines said it received no advance notice, and many passengers were moved to other flights.
  • For travelers: the Port of Seattle says it has no jurisdiction over ICE operations at the airport and was not involved; enforcement actions there happen without the Port's participation or knowledge.

Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles, in a scene the airline called "distressing" and Washington's governor denounced as out of control. Video of the incident, circulated on social media and by news outlets, showed officers in unmarked jackets struggling with at least one person on the ground as passengers with rolling suitcases looked on, and a woman screaming that her daughter was being taken and that she had a work permit, according to the Associated Press report carried by CNN.

What ICE says happened

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation at about 8 a.m. PST to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who, the agency said, "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws." During the confrontation, ICE said, another passenger threw hot coffee at the officers. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was also arrested; ICE said she had also overstayed her visa and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Reuters reported that it was not able to identify lawyers for either Mendoza or Mejia. The Associated Press noted that ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, particularly of people who overstayed visas in the past.

The airline and the airport respond

Alaska Airlines said ICE gave it no advance notice of the operation, which came during a busy travel weekend ahead of Thanksgiving. "We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests." Many passengers were put on other flights, and Flight 1306 itself departed at 11 a.m. PST, about three hours late. The Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said the arrest was distressing for the family and for surrounding passengers, that the operation took place without the Port's participation or knowledge, and that it is in conversation with the Department of Homeland Security about whether previously agreed protocols for enforcement at the airport were breached. FOX 13 reported it was the second known incident within a month in which ICE arrested multiple people at the airport.

"ICE is completely and totally out of control and today we are confronted with yet more evidence of this."

— Bob Ferguson, Governor of Washington

Political fallout

Governor Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the tactics "deeply un-American" at a Saturday news conference with labor leaders and local officials, said "the video is horrific and it is chilling," and called for ICE to be abolished. He told Alaska Airlines representatives, according to Reuters, that "they need to call on ICE to get out of our airports," and said he would make the same request of every airline serving Sea-Tac. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, said airport workers and passengers were already under strain and that the agents "introduced more fear and more chaos."

What travelers should know

Saturday's arrests were an enforcement action against named individuals, not a change to screening or boarding rules for other passengers, and the affected flight operated the same morning. The Port of Seattle notes on its website that it has no jurisdiction over ICE or Customs and Border Protection operations, and that some travelers using the airport have pending immigration applications. Travelers with a pending application or a past overstay who are flying domestically should understand that, based on the Associated Press's reporting, airports are now among the places ICE is actively making arrests — and should take legal advice about their own situation before traveling rather than relying on a domestic itinerary being low-risk.
